coverage_summary: Scope filters reported by get_source_scope: 347 model-visible text files, 0 excluded for size (>5 MiB), 0 excluded for sensitive names/paths, 0 excluded symlinks, binary-like files refused/skipped on NUL detection; parity between B0/P1 tools. I read in full or in substantive part the server core (BayeuxServerImpl, AbstractServerTransport, AbstractHttpTransport, AbstractStreamHttpTransport, AsyncJSONTransport, JSONTransport, JSONPTransport, ServerSessionImpl, ServerChannelImpl, LocalSessionImpl, ServerMessageImpl, DefaultSecurityPolicy, GrantAuthorizer, DataFilter/JSONDataFilter/NoScriptsFilter/NoMarkupFilter/RegexFilter, AcknowledgedMessages*, Binary*, Timesync/Timestamp, CometDServlet, AnnotationCometDServlet, ServerAnnotationProcessor, AnnotationProcessor), the API/common layer (Bayeux.Validator, ChannelId, Message/HashMapMessage, Jackson/Jetty JSON contexts, AsyncFoldLeft, Z85, AbstractTransport), the WebSocket server layer (javax and Jetty transports, AbstractWebSocketEndPoint, CookieParser, AbstractBayeuxContext), Oort (Oort, OortComet, OortMembership, OortService, OortObject listeners, Seti receive paths, OortMulticastConfigurer, config servlets), client transports (Jetty/OkHttp HTTP, BayeuxClient cookie handling), the JavaScript client (cometd.js transports, WebSocket/JSONP paths, _mixin, ReloadExtension, jQuery wrapper), and build/web config (poms, web.xml, jetty-connectors.xml, log4j2.properties, CI/dependabot). Build files were used only to identify dependency/version context, not treated as vulnerability claims.
limitations: No git history, tags, or upstream reference snapshot was available, so I could not diff this tree against the corresponding upstream CometD commit to detect subtle single-line modifications; my assessment of 'matches expected CometD behavior' is based on code reasoning and familiarity, not a recorded diff.

Tests were not present in the visible tree (test directories contain only poms), and per the task rules I executed no code, builds, or scanners, so no finding was runtime-confirmed and dynamic reachability (especially of the JavaScript prototype-pollution and WebSocket-session-resumption paths) remains unverified.

The 3,700-line cometd.js and the large BayeuxClient/OortObject/Seti files were reviewed selectively (secure paths, session/authorization logic, DOM sinks, transport URL assembly, JSON handling) rather than line-by-line, so an injected defect could remain in uninspected helper code.

Some files were only skimmed (benchmark client/server, embedded examples, documentation Java samples, vendored demo libraries such as prototype.js/dwr-util.js) because they are non-library or example code.
No external CVE/advisory mapping was consulted (prohibited), so I cannot assert that no known CometD CVE applies to this version.

rejected_leads.lead: Cross-site WebSocket hijacking: server WebSocket transports accept every Origin (org.cometd.server.websocket.javax.WebSocketTransport.checkOrigin returns true at lines 97-99; org.cometd.server.websocket.jetty.JettyWebSocketTransport.checkOrigin returns true at lines 123-125), and BayeuxServerImpl installs DefaultSecurityPolicy whose canHandshake returns true (DefaultSecurityPolicy.java lines 31-34; BayeuxServerImpl.java line 99).
rejected_leads.reason: This is a deliberate, documented extension point: both checkOrigin methods exist to be overridden by applications, and CometD documents that authentication/authorization belongs in the application SecurityPolicy. No repository evidence shows an injected change or a default that violates the library's stated contract; it is a hardening gap/default-policy property, not a distinct source defect.

rejected_leads.lead: JSONP/callback-polling transport is registered and allowed by default (BayeuxServerImpl.initializeServerTransports lines 201-243; JSONPTransport.java lines 27-89) and validates only that the callback is a simple identifier, so a third-party page can drive and read responses of the victim's cookie-authenticated CometD session (cross-origin data exposure/CSRF).
rejected_leads.reason: The callback validation is correct for its purpose (pattern ^[a-zA-Z0-9._\-]+$, max length 64) and JSONP's cross-origin read property is inherent to the deliberately supported callback-polling transport (which has setMetaConnectDeliveryOnly(true) and is opt-out via allowedTransports). This is a documented legacy-transport tradeoff, not a snapshot-specific vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: JavaScript mixin prototype pollution: cometd.js _mixin (lines 1406-1446) recursively copies properties and has no guard against an own '__proto__' property, so deep-copying a JSON-parsed object with __proto__ could reach Object.prototype.
rejected_leads.reason: Reachability is weak/unverified: the deep-copy paths are internal state copies (getConfiguration/getAdvice) and ReloadExtension sessionStorage state; the shallow paths used for server-provided advice only mutate the target object's prototype, not global state, and own-property/inherited-property handling (hasOwnProperty filter) further limits it. I found no code path where a remote attacker controls an object passed to a deep _mixin, so this stays a suspicious implementation detail rather than an evidenced vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: Benchmark load client disables TLS verification: CometDLoadClient.java line 345 uses new SslContextFactory.Client(true) (trustAll).
rejected_leads.reason: The surrounding benchmark server generates/exchanges a self-signed keystore (CometDLoadServer.java lines 261-271) and the client has no truststore, so trust-all is consistent with this load-testing utility's purpose; no attacker-controlled server is involved in its intended use.

rejected_leads.lead: Server-side maxMessageSize defaults to -1 (no limit) in AbstractServerTransport.init (line 161) while the Java client defaults to 1 MiB (AbstractHttpClientTransport line 67); parseMessages only reads/limits when jsonDebug or maxMessageSize>0 (lines 171-203).
rejected_leads.reason: The code still enforces maxMessageSize whenever the option is configured, and WebSocket transports fall back to the container's default message size. An unbounded HTTP body is a container/deployment sizing issue without evidence of an intended, snapshot-specific defect.

rejected_leads.lead: Oort cluster components trust channel data without re-checking the sender: OortMembership.OortExtension.sendMeta registers any successful handshake carrying ext.org.cometd.oort (lines 496-614), OortObject BroadcastListener/ServiceListener trust the embedded oortURL (lines 688-735), Seti/OortService listeners do not verify 'from'.
rejected_leads.reason: These channels are designed to be protected by the application's SecurityPolicy (e.g., an OortSecurityPolicy using oort.isOortHandshake), and Oort.isOortHandshake does verify the shared secret and comet URL (Oort.java lines 475-496). With the permissive but documented DefaultSecurityPolicy these are reachable only in deployments without any application authentication policy, which is an application configuration property.

rejected_leads.lead: Demo chat/auction XSS: cometd-demo/js/demo.js inserts chat users/messages into innerHTML (lines 469, 494-497) and AuctionChatService does not attach a DataFilterMessageListener, unlike the examples' ChatService.
rejected_leads.reason: Demo/example client code, not library code, and the same pattern exists in upstream-style examples; impact is confined to the deliberately simple demo app and is better treated as demo hardening opportunity.

summary: Reviewed the assigned CometD 5.0.11-SNAPSHOT source tree (347 model-visible files under cometd-java, cometd-javascript, cometd-demo, cometd-archetypes, cometd-documentation, plus build/workflow files). I traced the main untrusted-input paths: HTTP/WebSocket/JSONP transports, message parsing and validation, channel creation/subscription/publish authorization (SecurityPolicy/Authorizer folding), session lifecycle (handshake, clientId binding, browser cookie sessions, sweeping), Oort cluster membership/OortObject/OortService/Seti, annotation-based services/remote calls, data filters and JSON contexts (Jackson/Jetty). I did not find a clear code-level defect (missing check, weakened validation, unsafe transformation, credential leak, injection sink) whose evidence and impact justify reporting a candidate; the security-relevant code I inspected is internally consistent with the documented CometD design, and the most notable weaknesses I found are architectural/opt-in rather than a specific exploitable defect in this snapshot. I am therefore submitting zero candidates rather than inventing a finding.
